section_1.title: The Ingredients: Linear Combinations and Span
section_1.content: Define a linear combination as scaling vectors and adding them together. Visualize 'Span' as the total reachable space (the 'territory') covered by these vectors. Prerequisite: Students must understand vector addition and scalar multiplication.
section_1.example: Imagine a robot at (0,0). With vector v1=(1,0) and v2=(0,1), the robot can reach any point in the 2D plane by combining steps: c1*v1 + c2*v2. The 'Span' is the entire 2D coordinate system.

section_2.title: The Redundancy Test: Linear Dependence
section_2.content: Explain linear dependence as a 'wasteful' vector. If one vector can be formed by a combination of the others, it provides no new 'territory.' Graphically, this means vectors lie on the same line or plane.
section_2.example: If you have a robot with arms pointing at (1,0), (0,1), and (1,1), the third arm is redundant because it's just the sum of the first two. It adds no new reach to the robot's capabilities.

section_3.title: The Efficiency Expert: Bases
section_3.content: Introduce the Basis as the 'minimal set' of vectors required to span a space. It must be linearly independent and span the space. Think of it as the most efficient instruction manual to describe any point in a space.
section_3.example: To describe any position in a 3D room, you only need 3 specific vectors (the x, y, z axes). These 3 vectors form a basis. Adding a 4th vector would make the description 'dependent' and unnecessarily complex.

section_4.title: Synthesis and Summary
section_4.content: Quick recap: Linear combination (the action), Span (the reach), Dependence (the overlap), and Basis (the minimal toolset).
section_4.example: Imagine a toolkit: 'Span' is all the things you can fix; 'Basis' is the minimum set of tools you need to fix everything without carrying extra weight.
